lines.text: FIELD STATION — HEARTHOLLOW. Survey sheets go up at first light. Pencil and blanks in the tin by the door. Sign for the sheet you take.

Pencil underneath, a worse pen: north gate for the Reach, not the west track, under water since the thaw. Under that, smaller, in the warden's hand: yes, and thank you. Below both, a column of initials.
FORAGE SIGN — MEADOW REACH. Know four signs: tracks, scrapes, castings, browse line.
MIGRATING: the season either side of this one. DORMANT: further off than that. Neither of those, and no sign on the ground, means the animal has gone.
One block of granite on the north rise, cut into branching antlers, taller than a person, set deep.
The turf has grown over the foot. The weather side is worn round and pale. On the sheltered side, cut shallow, a herd of six figures with a line running north out of them and off the edge.
Where the meadow grass banks against the foot, the stone is warm to the hand.
The southern stone is snapped off at about half its height.
What is left of the carving is hooves and the bottom of a line, and the line runs off the broken edge to the north. The break carries the same lichen as the rest of the stone, at the same depth.
A stone figure stands in the water off the dock rim, turned out toward the channel. Only the crown of the head is above water, and the carving there is finished down to the parting in the hair.
The shallows round it are clear to the bottom, down to the weed and the stones lying on it. The water directly under it is not, and the face does not come clear from the rim.
The water at the rim comes to a boot top. Six feet out it is over a person's head.
The second figure stands where the reeds thin, in shallower water than the one at the dock.
The eyes on this one were never cut.

It is turned back to face the dock figure, and the carving is the same so far as that one can be seen at all. Between the two of them the reed stops growing in a band about a boat wide, and the water inside the band is darker.
The causeway stone leans downhill toward the water.
The peat has banked against the uphill side of it, about as high as a knee. The weather has taken the top of the carving away. Below that, six figures, and a line running east out of them.
The shallower cut runs its full length. The deeper stops before the edge.
NIGHT MARKET — open dusk to dawn. Stalls sell silk, thread, dye, lamp oil, relight kits. The rent falls due the first night of the month, in coin.
Pinned under it on a scrap: the Webvern figure for the town canopy, midsummer. Eleven struck out, nine struck out, seven. Across that in ink, another hand: stop writing on my notice.

The forest has grown up around this stone. It is cut from the same granite as the stones out on the meadow. Two trunks stand hard against its sides, and both trunks have gone flat where they touch it.
There is no granite anywhere in these woods.

Six figures on the sheltered side, in the same order as the six on the marsh stone, with the line running east out of them. Where the nearer trunk has gone flat against the granite, the bark is dead a hand either side.
A low structure at the shaft head, built of curved plates fitted without mortar.
The plates have the colour of fired clay. They are not clay. Up close the grain runs the way bone runs, fired hard enough to come out that colour, and each plate is thicker through than a door.
Candles have been set along the joins. They have worn hollows into the plate underneath, and every hollow is black with soot.
The second shrine stands at the bottom of the deep workings, past the last ladder. The air down here has not moved in thirty-one years.
The shrine is warmer than the rock it stands on. It has no joins anywhere: a single plate, curving away on both sides, shoulder height, with no tool mark on the outside.

Cut across the face, in a lettering the mine gave up using: KILNBACK. The wax below the letters has built up, been cut back with a knife, and built up again. The face inside the letters is warmer than the face outside them.
Vent heat has glazed the windward face of this stone to a skin of glass, and the glass has crazed and lifted in patches the size of a hand.
The sheltered face has none of that, and the cutting there is sharp. Six figures on it, the line out of them running south-east. Ash lies thick out here, and none of it has caught in the cutting.
Most of this board has been torn away at the tacks. What survives of the printed half reads: PLATES THIS YEAR — NINE. A date under it, part torn.
The rest is later hands on the bare wood. One small: plates go out when the illustrators have time. Below that, in a slower hand, the shelf hours — afternoons, and most evenings.
This stone stands in open ground, with nothing higher than the grass for a quarter mile round it in any direction. There is no sheltered side.
The cutting is shallow the whole way round. Six figures again, and the line out of them runs up the face and off the top edge instead of across it.

The gate stone is the largest on the road up, about double the height of the one out in the vale. It is set into cut rock rather than into ground. This stone carries the herd on both faces, and none of the others does.
On the outward face the six are walking in. On the inward face the same six are standing, and the hooves are cut level with the ground line.
A second stone further up the road, left unfinished. The antlers are roughed out to about half their depth, and the face where the herd would go has not been cut at all.
Tools lie at the foot of it under the ash: a hammer and three wedges, side by side. The ash over them takes a boot in to the ankle.
Nine stones at the caldera heart, evenly spaced, every one facing in toward the middle. All of them are carved, and the carving on these is not a herd.
Each stone carries one animal on its own, cut to double the size of the figures on the stones outside. The grass inside the ring is short and even.
The grass elsewhere in the Sanctum Fallow stands to the knee. Inside the ring it has been grazed down level. The dung lying on it has not dried out.
The stag comes down into the ring from the high side of the caldera. It does not hurry.
It is a Vellsire. The branching on its antlers is the branching cut on every stone from Meadow Reach up to here, and the spread is wider than a person is tall.
It stops in the middle of the ring, on the short grass, and puts its head up. It is standing side on to the rim, about a snare's throw from where the path comes in.
